fields.foundation: The Rashidun Caliphate began with a succession crisis. The Prophet Muhammad died in Medina in June 632 CE without a universally acknowledged successor, and the uncertainty threatened to dissolve the young Muslim community before it had consolidated control over the Arabian Peninsula. At the Saqifah of the Banu Sa’ida, a covered hall in Medina, leading companions debated the succession within hours of the Prophet’s death and acclaimed Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Muhammad’s close companion and father-in-law, as the first caliph, from the Arabic khalifa, “successor” or “deputy”. This set a precedent of selection by consultation that distinguished early Islamic government from both Byzantine dynastic monarchy and Sasanian sacral kingship. It also began the dispute over legitimate succession that would eventually divide the community into Sunni and Shia traditions. Abu Bakr’s first task was to keep the community in being. Much of Arabia rose in the Ridda Wars, the wars of “apostasy” and secession, as tribes that had submitted to Muhammad treated his death as ending their obligations and rallied around rival prophetic claimants such as Musaylima in Yamama, Tulayha among the Banu Asad and Sajah of the Banu Tamim. Abu Bakr divided his forces into several columns, traditionally eleven, and fought the Ridda Wars relentlessly in 632–633 CE, ending with the hard-fought Battle of Yamama, where Musaylima was killed. The wars reunified Arabia under caliphal authority and turned the energy of a now-united Arabian warrior society outward towards the wealthy settled empires of the north. Abu Bakr died of illness in 634 CE and was succeeded by Umar ibn al-Khattab. The transition preserved continuity while greatly quickening the pace of conquest, as Umar turned tribal raiding into systematic imperial expansion.
fields.socioeconomy: In its twenty-nine years the Rashidun Caliphate’s economic base changed from the pastoralism and limited agricultural surplus of Arabia to the administration of two of the most productive agrarian economies of the ancient world: the Sasanian irrigated lowlands of Mesopotamia and the Byzantine agricultural zones of Egypt and the Levant. Conquered territories were administered according to a fiscal principle associated with Umar that had large consequences for Islamic economic history. Umar did not distribute conquered farmland among Arab warriors as private property. He decreed that the lands of Iraq, Egypt and Syria would remain with their existing cultivators, who paid the kharaj, a land tax, to the treasury, while Arab warriors received stipends through the diwan, a register of soldiers and pensioners that Umar established in the late 630s or early 640s and that became the state’s principal mechanism for distributing wealth. This system kept conquered agriculture productive and channelled its surplus into stipends that sustained the Arab military establishment in purpose-built garrison cities, Kufa and Basra in Iraq and Fustat in Egypt, which were at once military camps, administrative centres and growing commercial hubs. The jizya, a poll tax on non-Muslim subjects, generated further revenue and created a fiscal disincentive to mass conversion, since widespread conversion would have reduced income, though this was never formal policy. Trade benefited from the removal of the frontier and its tolls that had long divided the Byzantine and Sasanian worlds. The result was a unified commercial space from the Nile to the borders of Central Asia that stimulated long-distance exchange in textiles, grain, metals and luxury goods.
fields.military: The Rashidun conquests were one of the most rapid expansions in pre-gunpowder history. They destroyed the Sasanian Empire, ended Byzantine power permanently in Syria, Palestine, Egypt and Cyrenaica, and extended Arab authority from Libya to the frontiers of Central Asia and the borders of Sind, all within about a quarter of a century and by a society with no prior tradition of imperial warfare or administration. The Arab armies were tribal forces of infantry and light cavalry, mounted on camels for strategic movement. Their advantage did not lie in technology, for they lacked the heavy cavalry and siege engineering of their Byzantine and Sasanian opponents. It lay in cohesion and motivation, mobility in desert conditions and the exhaustion that the great Byzantine-Sasanian war of 602–628 had inflicted on both empires. In the west, at the Battle of the Yarmuk in August 636 CE, Arab forces under the command of Abu Ubayda and Khalid ibn al-Walid, perhaps the most gifted battlefield commander of the seventh century, defeated a large Byzantine army over six days, in tradition aided by a dust storm. The victory delivered Syria permanently to Arab control; Jerusalem surrendered soon afterwards, and Egypt was conquered by Amr ibn al-As between 640 and 642 CE. In the east, the Battle of al-Qadisiyyah in 636 or 637 CE, where Saad ibn Abi Waqqas defeated the larger army of the Sasanian general Rostam Farrokhzad after several days of fighting, opened Iraq to conquest and was followed by the fall of the Sasanian capital Ctesiphon. The Battle of Nihawand in 642 CE, remembered in Islamic tradition as the “Victory of Victories”, broke the last organised Sasanian field army.
fields.governance: While it was still expanding, the Rashidun Caliphate built a framework capable of governing conquered populations of very different linguistic, religious and cultural backgrounds. Arab tribal tradition offered little precedent for this, and the four caliphs and their advisers had to improvise institutions. Umar ibn al-Khattab, whose ten-year caliphate from 634 to 644 CE saw the greatest volume of conquest, also did most to build them: he established the diwan, organised the garrison cities, appointed provincial governors (amirs) with defined jurisdictions and answerable to Medina, appointed judges (qadis) in major centres, and adopted the Islamic lunar calendar for official dating, anchoring it to the hijra of 622 CE. Under Uthman ibn Affan, caliph from 644 to 656 CE, the Quranic text was standardised into a single authoritative recension. Copies were sent to the major provincial centres while variant codices were ordered destroyed, and this recension became the textual foundation of Islamic law and theology. The legal system of this period drew on Quranic injunctions, remembered prophetic practice, later systematised as hadith, and the reasoned judgement (ijtihad) of the companions, without the elaborated schools of jurisprudence that developed under the Abbasids. Ali ibn Abi Talib’s troubled caliphate from 656 to 661 CE was dominated by the First Fitna, the civil war between Ali and the governor of Syria, Muawiya ibn Abi Sufyan, over responsibility for Uthman’s murder. It showed that the caliphate lacked mechanisms for resolving elite political conflict without resort to arms.
fields.impact: The Rashidun Caliphate’s twenty-nine years began a transformation of the Middle East, North Africa and western Iran whose consequences are still visible in the religious and cultural geography of the world fourteen centuries later. Arabic replaced Greek, Aramaic and Coptic as the dominant language of the Levant, Mesopotamia and Egypt. The process unfolded over the following centuries, with Arabic becoming the language of administration under the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik around 700 CE, but it was set in motion by the Rashidun conquests, and it created the Arabic-speaking world of today. The destruction of the Sasanian Empire was total and permanent. The Byzantine Empire survived the loss of its eastern provinces and endured until 1453 CE, but the Sasanian state ceased to exist with the death of Yazdegerd III in 651 CE. This ended over four centuries of Sasanian rule and turned Persian civilisation towards an Islamic framework within which it would later flourish as a major creative force. Conquered non-Muslim populations were treated as protected peoples (dhimmis), who were guaranteed security of life, property and worship in return for paying the jizya and accepting certain legal disabilities. This model of regulated religious pluralism, despite its inequalities, allowed the relatively rapid stabilisation of conquered territories. The dispute begun by the succession crisis, over whether legitimate leadership belonged to the Prophet’s family or rested on the community’s choice, produced the Sunni-Shia divide that has run through Islamic history ever since.
fields.decline: The Rashidun Caliphate was brought down almost entirely by internal political and religious conflict, not external military defeat, which is unusual among the empires in this dataset. At the moment of its collapse it faced no neighbouring power capable of threatening its survival. The origins of the conflict lay in the founding succession at the Saqifah. Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Prophet’s cousin and son-in-law, whom a significant part of the community believed Muhammad had designated as his successor, was passed over, and Ali’s partisans, the proto-Shia, never accepted the legitimacy of the caliphates of Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman. Violence at the summit had already begun with Umar’s assassination by a Persian slave in 644 CE. Uthman then appointed members of his Umayyad clan, the Banu Umayya, who had been among the Prophet’s most determined Meccan opponents before their late conversion, to major provincial governorships. This aroused mounting opposition and alienated early companions and garrison-city warriors who felt their contributions were being overlooked. In June 656 CE rebels, many of them from Egypt, broke into Uthman’s house in Medina and, according to tradition, killed him while he was reading the Quran. It was the first murder of a caliph by fellow Muslims in revolt, and it shattered the principle of caliphal inviolability and triggered the First Fitna. Ali’s caliphate was consumed by war against Aisha, the Prophet’s widow, and her allies Talha and al-Zubayr at the Battle of the Camel in 656 CE, and against Muawiya at the inconclusive Battle of Siffin in 657 CE. The agreement to arbitration at Siffin was repudiated by the Kharijites, who held that human arbitration of a divine question was illegitimate; one of them, Ibn Muljam, assassinated Ali in the mosque at Kufa in January 661 CE. Hasan ibn Ali’s subsequent abdication in favour of Muawiya ended the Rashidun principle of consultative selection and began the hereditary Umayyad Caliphate, which changed Islamic government from its experimental early phase into a dynastic imperial model.
fields.summary: In twenty-nine years the Rashidun Caliphate destroyed one ancient empire and stripped another of its richest provinces, permanently changed the religious and linguistic geography of three continents, and produced the disputes over legitimate authority and succession that have structured Islamic political thought and sectarian identity from the seventh century to the present day.
fields.teaser: Led by the first four caliphs after Muhammad, the Rashidun Caliphate (632–661) conquered Syria, Egypt, Iraq and the Sasanian Persian Empire in one of the fastest expansions in history.
fields.t0: The Rashidun Caliphate was the rule of the first four caliphs after the Prophet Muhammad, from Medina, in 632–661.
fields.t1: In about 25 years it destroyed the Sasanian Empire and took Syria and Egypt from Byzantium, setting Arabic on its path to dominance.
fields.t2: Disputes over succession led to the murders of three caliphs and civil war, ending in the hereditary Umayyad Caliphate.
fields.dyk: Umar adopted the Islamic lunar calendar for official dating, anchoring it to the hijra of 622, the system still used in the Muslim world today.
